title: South African Apartheid and U.S. Racial Discrimination
text:
South African Apartheid and U.S. Racial Discrimination

# South African Apartheid and U.S. Racial Discrimination

August 25, 2026

 Lwando Xaso 

 South African Apartheid and U.S. Racial Discrimination 

- Further Reading
- The Other Legacy: A Counternarrative to Celebrating America 250

“I come here this evening because of my deep interest and affection for a land settled by the Dutch in the mid-seventeenth century, then taken over by the British, and at last independent; a land in which the native inhabitants were at first subdued, but relations with whom remain a problem to this day; a land which defined itself on a hostile frontier; a land which has tamed rich natural resources through the energetic application of modern technology; a land which was once the importer of slaves, and now must struggle to wipe out the last traces of that former bondage. I refer, of course, to the United States of America.” 1 

This is the disarming introduction to the prominent address delivered by U.S. Senator Robert F. Kennedy in apartheid South Africa on June 6, 1966. Through his use of effective rhetorical misdirection, Kennedy skillfully draws a historical and cultural comparison between the United States and apartheid South Africa at a time when many Americans would have preferred to believe the two nations were fundamentally different.

The comparison might have been particularly offensive to Americans at the time because apartheid was internationally recognized as an exceptionally severe form of racial oppression, so much so that it led to annual condemnations by the U.N. General Assembly beginning in 1952 and regular U.N. Security Council denunciations after 1960. 2 And in December 1966, six months after Kennedy’s speech, the General Assembly officially condemned apartheid as a crime against humanity. 3 This type of global censure would have been unfamiliar to the U.S. despite its own notorious institutionalized racially oppressive system.

While the global solidarity of Black liberation movements is well documented and understood today, history often overlooks the high level of coordination among international networks of white supremacists who inspired one another to advance racial oppression. Kennedy’s introduction alludes to the interconnectedness of global racism by cleverly linking the ideological roots of South African apartheid to America’s racial discrimination.

Race relations in the U.S. and South Africa remain a problem 60 years after Kennedy’s address. The legacies of Jim Crow in the U.S and apartheid in South Africa are evident today in entrenched disparities in wealth, housing, and education and the overall systematic disadvantages that the Black populations in each country continue to face. However, post-apartheid South Africa has taken a different route than the U.S. in reckoning with its unjust history. South Africa made significant and somewhat unprecedented choices in, for example, establishing a Truth and Reconciliation Commission 4 and drafting a transformative constitution enshrining justiciable socioeconomic rights to directly address historical traumas and inequality, choices that are conspicuously absent from the American experience. However, these choices have not been a panacea. Today, South Africa manifests rampant inequality, dispossession, injustice and exclusion, but what is different is that it has a legitimate and progressive constitutional apparatus and the principles and values to address these societal ills. Yes, the struggle continues, but it continues under more enabling conditions. 5 

A critical part of the struggle today is the ability to draw appropriate lessons from history, which is, in some respects, discouraged. For example, comparing the American brand of racial hierarchy to other more universally maligned repressive regimes remains deeply controversial, as evidenced by efforts to remove Isabel Wilkerson’s book Caste: The Origins of Our Discontents from select school districts and libraries in the U.S. due to its well-supported claims that Nazi Germany sent its researchers to the U.S. to study Jim Crow for insights on how it subordinated and subjugated its Black population. 6 

Not only did Jim Crow inspire Nazi Germany, but it also inspired apartheid South Africa. Wilkerson points out that although people often use apartheid to convey the most extreme form of segregation, Jim Crow preceded apartheid. 7 

The highly moralized debate surrounding anti-miscegenation clearly demonstrates how Jim Crow served as a crucial precedent for the architects of apartheid South Africa. The enactment of anti-miscegenation legislation was critical to the apartheid state. By legally enforcing “racial purity,” they provided the foundational justification for the broader and elaborate framework of apartheid laws. Less than a year after the 1948 South African elections, which had formally established apartheid rule in South Africa, the apartheid regime’s minister of home affairs, Theophilus E. Dönges, wasted no time in introducing a bill to prohibit miscegenation.

Anthropologist Sebastian Jackson of the University of Virginia has shown that apartheid legislators directly referenced and utilized Jim Crow anti-miscegenation laws to construct the Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act of 1949 and the Immorality Amendment Act of 1950. According to Jackson, “While these ‘cornerstone’ policies of apartheid developed from local socio-political conflicts and economic tensions, they were always entangled in global racial formations, rooted in trans-oceanic histories of slavery, dispossession, and segregation.” 8 

In the 1930s, Afrikaner nationalist groups, who would become staunch supporters of apartheid, campaigned heavily for state bans on interracial relationships. The government of that time — to ensure its political survival — appeased these Afrikaner nationalists by establishing the De Villiers Commission, tasked with studying the “detrimental” socioeconomic effects of interracial marriages and intimacies. In Jackson’s work, we see how the De Villiers Commission’s methodology included studying American laws on miscegenation, providing apartheid legislators with policy blueprints from which they created laws of their own.

Jackson writes: “The De Villiers Commission contacted South Africa’s chief diplomat in Washington D.C., directing him and ‘practically the whole research staff’ to study American anti-miscegenation laws at the Library of Congress. They learned that thirty of America’s forty-eight states enforced anti-miscegenation laws, and they proposed that South African lawmakers could learn from these models.” 9 Even though the De Villiers Commission found that interracial relationships were rare, they still recommended banning them completely to ensure they did not grow in popularity. In reaching their conclusion, the De Villiers Commission pointed to the U.S. and Australia as examples of places where similar bans were working.

No action was taken on the recommendation of the De Villiers Commission until the formal advent of apartheid in 1948, when the regime’s minister of home affairs picked up where the De Villiers Commission left off.

Jackson’s work also highlights a parliamentary debate concerning the suggested anti-miscegenation legislation, explicitly referencing the remarks of a legislator recorded as M. Visser, who not only endorsed the minister’s proposed anti-miscegenation bill but also pointed to American Jim Crow segregation, stating, “It would be my pleasure to notify you that apartheid is already enforced in the southern states of America.” 10 

At the end of the parliamentary debate, the Minister concluded: “Look at the experiences of other countries regarding the same issue of mixed marriages. Is it not something for the opposition to consider that thirty of the forty-eight states in the United States have such policies in place? Is it not an argument to prove that there are no reasons to discard such laws, just because they may not be as efficient as we would like? I assume that those difficulties also exist there, but thirty states have decided to implement these laws; thirty states considered it necessary to take legislative action in order to keep this social evil under control. And, let me remind the honoured Members that the demographic proportions in the United States, in those thirty states, are not even half, not even a quarter, as urgent as the situation in South Africa.” 11 

Propelled by such reasoning, the Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act (1949) passed by a thin margin, becoming the first major legislation of the apartheid regime. The following year, the apartheid regime added an amendment to the Immorality Act of 1927, which had criminalized interracial sex outside of marriage between white and Black individuals, extending the prohibition to sex between white and all non-white people.

In contrast, almost a year after Kennedy’s visit to South Africa, the U.S. Supreme Court held that laws banning interracial marriage violated the Equal Protection and Due Process clauses of the 14th Amendment to the American Constitution. 12 As the U.S. loosened its segregationist laws, apartheid South Africa became more draconian.

Ernest Cole, Segregational Signs at a South African Train Station, 1972. (Copyright: public domain.)

The enforcement of the anti-miscegenation laws was left to the apartheid police, who often surveilled suspects to confirm compliance and raided the residences of suspected mixed-race couples. Participating in an illegal mixed marriage resulted in arrest and imprisonment. Officials who knowingly performed these outlawed ceremonies faced a heavy fine.

The anti-miscegenation laws were eventually repealed in 1985. And since the formal dismantling of apartheid in 1994, the odds of an individual marrying someone of the same race as them decreased from 303:1 in 1996, to 95:1 in 2011 — illustrating an increase in interracial marriages in South Africa. 13 

During Kennedy’s visit to South Africa, Prime Minister Hendrik Verwoerd, widely acknowledged as the architect of apartheid, refused to meet with him. Before becoming prime minister, Verwoerd served as the minister of native affairs responsible for orchestrating apartheid’s fundamental and extensive legislative framework, building upon the anti-miscegenation laws.

Verwoerd had left his career in academia in 1937 to transition into full-time politics and media. A seminal moment in his transition into politics was the American Carnegie Commission of Investigation on the Poor White Question in South Africa, a landmark sociological study that Verwoerd found compelling for a number of reasons, including the fact that he was previously a professor of sociology.

Hendrik Frensch Verwoerd as editor of the newspaper Die Transvaler, 1945. (Copyright: public domain.)

The Carnegie Commission began its work in 1929 and was at that time the largest and most complex social science study ever conducted in Africa. According to a 2004 reflection by the Carnegie Corporation, the inquiry became more than a sociological inquiry; it was a watershed event in South African social and political history. 14 Since the study was designed to set a precedent for similar future studies, two American sociologists — Kenyon L. Butterfield and C.W. Coulter — were brought in as consultants. Members of the Poor White Commission also included white South African academics, clergy and activists whose objective was to uplift nearly 300,000 impoverished Afrikaners, a crisis that threatened white political solidarity.

According to the Carnegie Corporation’s Report, the commission’s resulting five-volume report in 1932 was met with widespread praise and public discussion in newspapers.
